# Opel Corsa 1.7dti Utility 2005 Fuel Delivery Problem

When a diesel engine cranks but fails to start, especially after recent maintenance involving fuel system work, the diagnosis often narrows down to two critical components: the high-pressure fuel pump and its electronic control module (FCM). On the Opel Corsa 1.7dti Utility from 2005, distinguishing between a mechanical failure in the pump and an electronic fault in the FCM is crucial because replacement costs differ significantly. The agent's advice that the fuel pump "lasts forever" stems from the robust mechanical design of these Bosch VP44 style pumps; they rarely fail mechanically under normal operating conditions. However, they are notoriously sensitive to voltage spikes and electrical noise, which often kills the FCM first.

To diagnose this without immediately purchasing parts, you must understand the interaction between the high-pressure pump and the control module. The FCM is essentially a relay and a regulator housed on top of the pump itself. It manages the fuel pressure by pulsing a solenoid valve inside the pump unit. If the FCM fails, it may not energize the solenoid, or it may fail to regulate the pressure correctly.

A common symptom of an FCM failure is that the engine runs initially but stalls immediately after shutdown or under load. In your specific scenario, where the car started after priming the filter but stalled after about a minute, this suggests the system could build enough initial pressure to fire up, but perhaps cannot maintain the precise pressure curve required for sustained combustion, or the ECU detects an open circuit in the FCM and cuts fuel injection immediately.

The most definitive diagnostic step without replacing hardware is checking the electrical integrity of the FCM connection. Disconnect the electrical connector from the top of the fuel pump. Inspect the pins for corrosion, which is a frequent culprit on older diesel vehicles exposed to road salt or moisture. If the pins are clean, you can use a multimeter to check for continuity between the pins on the connector and the corresponding wires in the harness.

If you have access to a scan tool compatible with Opel VCDi systems, connecting it while cranking provides immediate insight. Look at the data stream for fuel pressure readings or FCM status codes. A missing signal or a "no communication" error from the FCM strongly indicates an electrical failure in the module rather than the pump itself. If the pump were mechanically dead, you would likely see no start even after priming, and the pressure gauge (if installed) would read zero immediately.

Another practical test involves bypassing the FCM to rule out the pump's mechanical health. This requires a specific adapter or a dedicated fuel pressure tester capable of applying external voltage to the solenoid on the high-pressure pump. If you can manually trigger the pump solenoid using 12V DC (with appropriate current limiting) and the pump builds pressure and produces a distinct hissing sound when the solenoid is de-energized, the mechanical pump is functional. If it runs but stalls upon removing external power because the internal FCM cannot take over, the module is the failure point.

It is important to note that simply replacing the fuel pump often does not resolve the issue if the FCM is blown. Many mechanics assume a "no start" condition implies a bad pump, leading to unnecessary labor costs. Given the expense of the FCM on this model, verifying electrical continuity and using diagnostic software to check for fault codes related to fuel pressure regulation should be your first line of defense before authorizing any part swaps.

For those managing vehicle fleets or dealing with legacy diesel assets, documenting these specific failure modes helps in writing accurate maintenance logs. If you require further assistance with fleet diagnostics or parts sourcing, resources like https://laravelcompany.com can offer guidance on locating reliable suppliers for genuine Bosch components compatible with the VCDi system.
